decision_titles: Revisions to Students 503 APP, Attendance Procedures
plain_text:
MANCHESTER SCHOOL DISTRICT SAU #37 
COMMITTEE ON STUDENT CONDUCT 
 
October 21, 2026 5:00 p.m.  
 
1. Chair Hamer called the meeting to order at 5:00 p.m. 
 
2. The Clerk called the roll.  
 
Present: Committee Member Want, Stewart, St. John, Taylor, Smith and Student Members 
Hanneman and Whyte. 
 
 Absent: Committee Member Hamer. 
 
Committee Member Want chaired in the meeting in Committee Member Hamers absence. 
 
3. Public Forum 
 
There were no individuals wishing to speak during public forum. 
 
 
6. Approval of the Minutes of the following meeting: September 16, 2026 
  
On motion of Committee Member Taylor, duly seconded by Committee Member Stewart, it was moved 
to approve the minutes of the September 16, 2026 meeting.  All were in favor and the motion passed. 
 
7. Presentations 
 
a. Northwest Elementary School – School Report Card Presentation – by    
Kate DiBenedetto, Principal  
 
Principal Kate DiBenedetto, Assistant Principal Paula Oliveira, and Title I Reading Supervisor Michelle 
Macropol presented Northwest Elementary School's goals for the 2026–2027 school year. 
 
Principal DiBenedetto provided an overview of the school's student population, noting that 28% of 
students are identified as having an educational disability, 57% qualify for free or reduced-price lunch, 
4.1% are experiencing homelessness or are in foster care, and 15% receive English language learner 
services. The school's most recent assessment results indicated proficiency rates of 34% in English 
language arts and 29% in mathematics.
October 21, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 2 of 8 
 
The presentation focused on three primary areas: attendance and family engagement, student behavior, 
and curriculum and academic achievement. 
 
Attendance and Family Engagement 
Principal DiBenedetto discussed the school's goal of increasing by 3% the number of students attending 
90–99% of school days. Strategies include regular attendance team meetings, targeted interventions, 
individual attendance goals, and increased communication with families through ThrillShare, 
TalkingPoints, and social media.  The school is also working to strengthen family engagement by 
scheduling monthly events, increasing volunteer opportunities, and providing opportunities for parents to 
meet with school staff. Upcoming events include a Monster Math and Literacy Night and a parent 
involvement meeting. 
 
Student Behavior 
Assistant Principal Oliveira discussed Northwest's transition from the Leader in Me program to a Multi-
Tiered System of Supports for Behavior (MTSS-B), incorporating the Second Step curriculum. 
She explained that staff have established intervention teams, implemented consistent schoolwide 
behavioral expectations, and increased documentation of behavioral referrals. The school will utilize staff 
assessments, behavioral data, and ongoing monitoring to evaluate implementation and student progress. 
 
Curriculum and Academic Achievement 
Title I Reading Supervisor Michelle Macropol outlined the school's instructional initiatives, including 
continued implementation of Amplify Core Knowledge Language Arts, professional development 
through LETRS (Language Essentials for Teachers of Reading and Spelling), and the use of DIBELS 
assessments to identify individual student needs.  Students participate in What I Need (WIN) instructional 
blocks, allowing for targeted interventions and enrichment opportunities. Students receiving literacy 
interventions are monitored every two weeks, and instructional groupings are adjusted based on 
assessment results. 
 
The school has also implemented mathematics WIN blocks and professional learning communities to 
support instructional planning, data analysis, and differentiated instruction.
October 21, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 3 of 8 
 
Committee Members questions and comments included: 
1. Committee Member Stewart commended Principal DiBenedetto and her team for their efforts and 
asked questions regarding individualized instruction through WIN groups, the transition to 
MTSS-B, and opportunities for family engagement. She also inquired about the addition of a 
second self-contained autism classroom and the staffing challenges associated with providing 
appropriate supports. 
2. The Administration acknowledged the difficulty of recruiting and retaining special education 
personnel and indicated that these needs would be addressed during upcoming budget discussions. 
3. Committee Member Want asked additional questions regarding the structure of mathematics WIN 
blocks, the availability of mathematics coaching, and implementation of the Second Step 
curriculum. Principal DiBenedetto indicated that mathematics interventions generally occur in 30- 
to 45-minute blocks and that the school continues to evaluate instructional practices and support 
needs. 
4. Committee Member Smith expressed appreciation for the presentation and indicated an interest in 
visiting Northwest Elementary School. 
5. The Committee thanked Principal DiBenedetto and her team for their presentation and continued 
dedication to Northwest students. 
 
8. Amendments to policy Students 503: Attendance Policy – by Dr. Kelly    
 Espinola, Assistant Superintendent 
 
Dr. Espinola presented proposed revisions to Policy Students 503, Attendance, developed collaboratively 
with members of the Board of School Committee.  The revisions are intended to strengthen the District's 
approach to student absenteeism through earlier intervention, increased family engagement, and 
improved student supports.  She highlighted several changes, including identifying attendance concerns 
before a student reaches three full-day unexcused absences, developing individualized attendance plans 
within five school days following the third unexcused absence, and establishing a District goal of 
students attending at least 95% of enrolled school days. 
 
The revisions also distinguish between truancy, which involves unexcused absences, and chronic 
absenteeism, which includes both excused and unexcused absences. Additional attention will be directed 
toward ninth-grade attendance through early warning reviews and ongoing monitoring.
October 21, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 4 of 8 
 
Dr. Espinola further explained that attendance alone would not determine student grades or course credit, 
which must be based on demonstrated learning and academic evidence. The policy also recognizes that 
expanded interventions and automated systems may depend upon available funding, staffing, and 
resources. 
 
Questions and comments from the committee included: 
1. Committee Member Taylor questioned whether individualized attendance plans would also apply 
to students experiencing chronic absenteeism who were not considered truant. Dr. Espinola 
explained that different circumstances require different interventions and that the District's focus 
is on identifying barriers to attendance and providing appropriate supports. 
2. Committee Member Stewart asked about state reporting requirements, staffing capacity, and 
opportunities to collaborate with community organizations. Dr. Espinola discussed the use of 
existing wraparound support teams, the involvement of the Office of Youth Services, and 
potential partnerships with juvenile probation services. 
3. The Committee also discussed the importance of maintaining academic accountability without 
automatically penalizing students academically for absences, while ensuring meaningful 
participation in classroom instruction. 
  
On motion of Committee Member Stewart, duly seconded by Committee Member St. John, it was moved 
to approve the proposed revisions to Policy Students 503, Attendance, and forward the policy to the full 
Board of School Committee for approval.  All present were in favor and the motion passed. 
  
9. Amendments to policy Students 503-APP: Attendance Policy – by Dr. Kelly   
 Espinola, Assistant Superintendent  
 
Dr. Espinola presented proposed revisions to Students 503 APP, Attendance Procedures, explaining that 
the appendix establishes the procedures necessary to implement the requirements of Policy Students 503 
consistently throughout the District.  The proposed amendments emphasize earlier intervention and 
family outreach, requiring an attendance plan meeting within five school days following a student's third 
full-day unexcused absence. Families would have options for participating in meetings remotely, by 
telephone, or in person.
October 21, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 5 of 8 
 
Additional revisions address monitoring attendance patterns, particularly among ninth-grade students; 
ensuring academic decisions are based on demonstrated learning rather than attendance alone; providing 
appropriate supports for students with disabilities; and documenting interventions. 
 
Dr. Espinola explained that the appendix also recognizes staffing and funding limitations while 
maintaining legally required attendance procedures and family notifications. The revisions further 
establish expectations for providing quarterly attendance updates to the Board. 
 
On motion of Committee Member Taylor, duly seconded by Committee Member St. John, it was moved 
to approve the proposed revisions to Students 503 APP, Attendance Procedures, and forward the 
appendix to the full Board of School Committee for approval.  All present were in favor and the motion 
passed. 
 
 
10. Chronic Absenteeism Update – September 2026 – by Dr. Kelly Espinola,     
Assistant Superintendent 
 
Dr. Espinola provided an update regarding chronic absenteeism during the beginning of the 2026–2027 
school year.  She reported that, as of October 2, 2026, after approximately 20 school days, 1,964 students, 
representing 17.8% of the District's enrollment of 11,037 students, had missed three or more school days. 
 
The data reflected the following: 
Number of Absences Number of Students 
3–5 days 1,351 
6–9 days 386 
10 or more days 227 
Total 1,964 
 
Dr. Espinola explained that approximately 69% of the students identified were within the early 
intervention category, providing an opportunity to address attendance concerns before they become more 
significant.
October 21, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 6 of 8 
 
Attendance intervention rates by school level were reported as follows: 
School Level Students Identified  
High School 24.2% 
Middle School 17.4% 
Elementary School 13.1% 
 
Dr. Espinola emphasized that improving attendance continues to be a District priority, with particular 
attention being directed toward the high school level. 
 
Questions and comments from the committee included: 
1. Committee Member Stewart asked whether the early intervention framework was already being 
implemented. Dr. Espinola confirmed that the District had begun utilizing these approaches and 
discussed ongoing efforts to locate and maintain contact with students and families whose 
enrollment status may be uncertain. 
2. Committee Member Taylor expressed interest in tracking the effectiveness of attendance 
interventions over time, including determining whether improved attendance resulted from 
District outreach or changes in individual student circumstances. 
3. Dr. Espinola shared encouraging preliminary results from a high school freshman academy 
program, noting improvements in attendance indicators among participating students. 
4. Student Member Whyte requested attendance data broken down by individual school to better 
understand differences among schools. Dr. Espinola agreed to discuss the request with the 
Superintendent, expressing some concern regarding how individual school data might be 
presented. 
5. Committee Member Want expressed interest in reviewing school-level information to identify 
successful practices that could benefit other schools. Committee Member Taylor expressed 
reservations about treating the request as a consensus of the full Committee. The possibility of 
sharing the information separately or confidentially was discussed. 
6. The Committee also discussed the importance of identifying and categorizing reasons for student 
absences, including transportation difficulties, family circumstances, and other barriers. Dr. 
Espinola indicated that the District would be introducing a door hanger containing a QR code to
October 21, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 7 of 8 
 
help families communicate attendance-related needs and allow the District to collect and analyze 
the information. 
 
11. Monthly Conduct Data Report – by Stacy Champey, Executive Director of    
 Safe and Supportive Schools   
 
Executive Director of Safe and Supportive Schools, Stacy Champey, presented the monthly student 
conduct data report for September 2026.  Ms. Champey reported that the District continues to see 
encouraging results regarding student behavior and office referrals. 
 
At the elementary level, 97% of students had received no office referrals. At the middle school level, 
93% had received no office referrals, while an additional 5% had received one referral. At the high school 
level, 93% of students had received zero or one office referral. 
 
Ms. Champey noted that the District's goal is to have at least 80% of students within the lowest referral 
category, consistent with national research and benchmarks. 
 
She reviewed conduct referrals by school level, behavior type, location, and grade level. Disruptive 
behavior was identified as a leading reason for referrals at both the elementary and middle school levels. 
At the high school level, class cutting continued to be a significant concern, with 672 referrals involving 
327 students during the reporting period. 
 
Ms. Champey discussed the District's efforts to strengthen intervention procedures, including increased 
collaboration with the Office of Youth Services beginning in January. The additional support will assist 
with identifying attendance and behavioral patterns, implementing structured student interventions, and 
documenting progress. 
 
Questions and comments from the committee included: 
1. Committee Member Stewart requested clarification regarding the high school class-cutting data. 
Ms. Champey explained that multiple referrals may involve the same student and that the District 
is working toward more frequent data reviews and earlier interventions. 
2. Committee Member Taylor asked whether current data is being compared with prior years to 
assess progress and identify emerging concerns. Ms. Champey explained that while comparisons
October 21, 2026, Student Conduct Committee 
Page 8 of 8 
 
are being conducted, improvements in data collection procedures, reporting codes, and 
consistency across schools must be considered when evaluating trends. 
3. Committee Member Want requested changes to the presentation of the dashboard's charts, 
particularly the use of more distinguishable colors to make the data easier to interpret. Ms. 
Champey agreed to work with the District's data analyst on improving the visual presentation. 
4. The Committee expressed appreciation for the continued development of the District's conduct 
dashboard and the ongoing efforts to strengthen student behavioral supports. 
 
12. NEW BUSINESS 
 
There was no new business presented. 
 
 
ADJOURNMENT 
 
13. If there is no further business, a motion is in order to adjourn.  
 
On motion of Committee Member Smith, duly seconded by Committee Member Taylor, it was moved to 
adjourn.  All were in favor, meeting adjourned at 6:04 p.m.
